01 · Why monitor
Metrics are readings; monitoring turns readings into decisions
Metric
A number measured over time
Heart rate, step count, CPU %, requests per second
Blue: the series · dashed: the alert threshold · dot: the spike
Monitoring
A loop that watches metrics and acts
Collect · read the numbers on a schedule
Store · keep the history to learn what is normal
Visualise · see trends and changes
Alert · notify when a rule is broken
Act · fix, scale, or tune the rule
Analogy: a step counter gives a metric; checking it daily against a goal is monitoring

01 · Why monitor
Prometheus became the default way to monitor cloud-native systems
2012
Started at SoundCloud; open source, Apache 2.0
2nd
CNCF project to graduate, after Kubernetes (2018)
v3.15
Current release (Sept 2026), the version our lab installs
Pull model
Targets expose /metrics; Prometheus fetches on a schedule
Labels
Every series carries dimensions: pod, node, status code
PromQL
One language to query, aggregate, graph and alert
Dynamic targets
Service discovery follows pods as they come and go
Sources: prometheus.io · CNCF (graduated Aug 2018) · github.com/prometheus/prometheus releases (v3.15.0, 24 Sep 2026)

02 · How Prometheus works
One server does the core work; four helpers feed it and act on it
Core · Prometheus server
Retrieval scrapes targets · TSDB stores the series on local disk · HTTP server answers PromQL
In · where metrics come from
Exporters translate third-party systems into metrics · Pushgateway holds metrics from short-lived jobs · Service discovery (Kubernetes, files) lists the targets
Out · who uses the data
Alertmanager groups and routes alerts to email or Slack · Grafana, the Prometheus UI and API clients query with PromQL
Rule of thumb: everything is pulled by the server, except alerts, which it pushes to Alertmanager.
Diagram: course notes (Monitoring README)

02 · How Prometheus works
Prometheus pulls metrics on a schedule; only short-lived jobs push
Service discovery
Kubernetes API
Prometheus server
Retrieval → TSDB
node-exporter :9100
kube-state-metrics :8080
Pushgateway :9091
Short-lived job
e.g. a nightly backup
Why push at all? A batch job may finish before the next scrape. It pushes to the Pushgateway, which Prometheus then scrapes like any target.
What a target serves at /metrics
# HELP http_requests_total Requests # TYPE http_requests_total counter http_requests_total{code="200"} 1027 http_requests_total{code="500"} 3 # TYPE node_load1 gauge node_load1 0.42
Plain text over HTTP: any app can expose it.
Prometheus adds its own series per target: up = 1 if the last scrape worked, 0 if not.

02 · How Prometheus works
Every time series is a metric name plus a set of labels
node_cpu_seconds_total{cpu="0", mode="idle", instance="10.0.0.5:9100"}  18342.7
metric name: what is measured
label keys
label values
sample value (with a timestamp)
Counter
Only goes up; resets to 0 on restart
http_requests_total
Query with rate()
Gauge
Goes up and down
node_load1
Use the value directly
Histogram
Counts observations in buckets
request_seconds_bucket
Percentiles via histogram_quantile()
Summary
Quantiles computed in the app
rpc_duration_seconds
Cannot be aggregated across pods
Cardinality: every new label value creates a new series. Label by status code, method or pod; never by user ID, email or request ID.

02 · How Prometheus works
The TSDB keeps recent data fast and old data compact
Head block + WAL
last ~2 h in memory; write-ahead log on disk
2-hour blocks
immutable chunks + index written to disk
Compaction
merges small blocks into larger ones
Retention
old blocks deleted: 15 days by chart default
remote_write
stream samples to Thanos · Grafana Mimir · Cortex for months of history and a global view
Single node by design
for high availability, run two identical servers scraping the same targets
Source: prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage · chart default retention: prometheus-community/prometheus values.yaml

02 · How Prometheus works
PromQL in four moves: select, rate, aggregate, shape
STEP 1
Select
node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}
Pick the series: idle CPU seconds, per core
STEP 2
Rate
rate(…{mode="idle"}[5m])
Counter → per-second rate over 5 minutes
STEP 3
Aggregate
avg by (instance) (rate(…{mode="idle"}[5m]))
Average the cores: one value per node
STEP 4
Shape
100 * (1 - avg by (instance) (rate(…[5m])))
Idle fraction → busy %
rate()
counters only
sum / avg / max by
collapse labels you don't need
topk(5, …)
the worst offenders
… > 80
a comparison = an alert condition

02 · How Prometheus works
Prometheus decides when to alert; Alertmanager decides who hears
Alerting rule
a PromQL condition, checked every interval
Pending → Firing
true for the whole for: window
Alertmanager
groups · dedupes · silences · routes
Email
Slack
PagerDuty
- alert: HighNodeCPU   expr: |     100 * (1 - avg by (instance) (rate(       node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]     ))) > 80   for: 10m   labels: {severity: warning}   annotations:     summary: "High CPU on {{ $labels.instance }}"
Alertmanager adds
Grouping · 50 pod alerts arrive as one message
Inhibition · node down mutes its pod alerts
Silences · mute during planned maintenance
Routing · by label to the right team and channel

03 · Grafana
Start every dashboard with the same few signals
Infrastructure · USE method: every node and cluster
Utilisation
CPU busy
1 - avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]))
Saturation
Load per core
node_load1 / count by (instance) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"})
Errors
Pods not running
count by (namespace) (kube_pod_status_phase{phase=~"Pending|Failed"} == 1)
Services · RED method: needs an instrumented app
Rate
Requests / s
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
Errors
5xx ratio
sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
Duration
p95 latency
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
USE: Brendan Gregg · RED: Tom Wilkie · Golden signals: Google SRE book

04 · Hands-on lab
Steps 1–2: a running cluster and the Helm package manager
# Step 1 · start a local Kubernetes cluster minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8g kubectl get nodes # expect: minikube Ready control-plane # Step 2 · install Helm sudo snap install helm --classic helm version # macOS: brew install helm # Windows: winget install Helm.Helm
minikube
A real single-node Kubernetes cluster on your laptop. Extra CPU and memory keep all six monitoring pods schedulable.
Helm
The package manager for Kubernetes. One chart = dozens of manifests, versioned, configurable with values, removable in one command.
Check before moving on
Node is Ready and helm version prints a version.

04 · Hands-on lab
Step 4: expose the Prometheus UI and confirm every target is up
Your browser
localhost or minikube IP
Service prometheus-server-ext
type NodePort
prometheus-server pod
container port :9090
# expose the server as a NodePort service kubectl expose service prometheus-server \   --name=prometheus-server-ext --type=NodePort \   --port=9090 --target-port=9090 # option A · minikube prints a URL minikube service prometheus-server-ext --url # option B · port-forward (WSL, remote VM) kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus-server-ext \   9090:9090 --address=0.0.0.0
Check
Status → Target health: every job UP. Then run up in the Query tab.
Caution
--address=0.0.0.0 listens on every interface and Prometheus has no login. Use it on a trusted network only, or drop the flag (localhost).

04 · Hands-on lab
Step 5a: three queries that answer "are my nodes healthy?"
Question
PromQL · paste into the Query tab
Expect
Is every target being scraped?
up
One row per target; 1 = scrape OK, 0 = failing
How busy is each node's CPU?
100 * (1 - avg by (instance) (   rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])))
One line per node, 0–100 %; low on an idle cluster
How much memory is in use?
100 * (1 - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes          / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes)
Memory in use, % per node
18
04 · Hands-on lab
Step 5b: kube-state-metrics answers "what is running where?"
Question
PromQL · paste into the Query tab
Expect
Which pods are running?
kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"}
One series per pod: 1 if Running, else 0
How many pods are running?
count(kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1)
A single number
How many per namespace?
count by (namespace) (   kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1)
One number each: default, kube-system, …
Try it live: run kubectl create deploy demo --image=nginx --replicas=3, switch to the Graph tab and watch the count rise.

04 · Hands-on lab
Step 6a: install Grafana from its new community Helm repository
helm repo add grafana-community \   https://grafana-community.github.io/helm-charts helm repo update helm install grafana grafana-community/grafana # admin password, stored in a Kubernetes secret kubectl get secret --namespace default grafana \   -o jsonpath="{.data.admin-password}" | base64 --decode ; echo kubectl expose service grafana --name=grafana-ext \   --type=NodePort --target-port=3000 minikube service grafana-ext --url
New repository
grafana/grafana is deprecated; the chart moved to grafana-community (30 Jan 2026)
Open grafana-ext
minikube service needs the NodePort copy, not the original service
No persistence
dashboards live in the pod and vanish on restart (fix: slide 22)
Keep it secret
never paste the password in slides or chat; rotate it if you did

Step 6b: connect Grafana to Prometheus and import dashboards
1

Data source URL
http://prometheus-server.default.svc.cluster.local
Grafana runs inside the cluster, so it reaches Prometheus by service DNS: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local on the Service port 80. No NodePort or port-forward needed.

04 · Hands-on lab
When the lab breaks, it is almost always one of five things
Symptom
Check
Fix
Pods stuck Pending
kubectl describe pod <name>
Not enough CPU or memory: recreate with minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8g
Target shows DOWN
Status → Target health: read the error column
Pod not ready yet or wrong port: check kubectl get pods
Grafana panel: No data
Data source Save & test; dashboard time range
Use the in-cluster URL; set range to Last 15 minutes
minikube service URL won't open
WSL, Docker driver or a remote VM?
Use kubectl port-forward and open localhost
Dashboards gone after restart
kubectl get pvc shows none
--set persistence.enabled=true or export dashboard JSON

05 · Production and recap
Same building blocks in production, with five upgrades
Area
Lab today
Production
Install
Two separate charts
kube-prometheus-stack: Operator, ServiceMonitors, built-in dashboards and alert rules
Access & security
NodePort and port-forward, no auth
Ingress + TLS + SSO; Kubernetes RBAC; network policies
Storage
Pod disk, 15 days
Persistent volumes + remote_write to Thanos or Mimir
Availability
One replica of everything
2+ Prometheus replicas; clustered Alertmanager
Alerting
Default rules, no receivers
Per-service rules with runbooks; on-call routing
kubectl create namespace monitoring helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring
23
05 · Production and recap
Three ideas to take away
1
Prometheus pulls, stores and alerts
Labelled time series scraped from exporters found by service discovery
2
PromQL is the one language
Select, rate, aggregate, shape: the same query graphs and alerts
3
Grafana makes it visible
Data source + dashboards; Helm makes the whole stack a short install
Clean-up
helm uninstall grafana prometheus kubectl delete svc \   prometheus-server-ext grafana-ext minikube delete
